generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, Kolb's cycle is familiar ground: experiential learning underpins placements and practical work across the subjects, from clinic hours in sport therapy to coaching placements, and reflective logs are often assessed against it. The point for your own reflection is Kolb's point: an experience, a rehab plan that did not progress, a session that felt flat, becomes a source of learning only when you turn what you noticed into something you will do differently. A reflection that understands the problem but changes nothing has stopped one step short.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport therapy students have each reflected well on why a rehabilitation case study lost marks, and reach the same understanding: they wrote up their treatment notes from memory, days after the clinic session, and left out details needed to repeat the plan. Now each decides what to do about it.

Tom resolves to take the case notes more seriously next time and to be more careful recording the treatment. This is a genuine intention, but it is not an action: there is nothing specific to carry out, and 'more careful' could mean anything. Next time will probably look much like last time.

Amara decides to complete the treatment notes during the clinic session itself, filling a standard SOAP template at each stage before the client leaves. That is a concrete action: it names what to do and when, it follows directly from the reflection, and it would genuinely change the next case study. The loop is closed.

Both understood the problem equally well. Only Amara turned that understanding into something that will actually change the next attempt.
generatedProse.summary: A reflective cycle is complete only when it produces a concrete action: something specific you will do differently, not a vague intention to improve. Kolb's cycle shows why, treating experience as the source of learning only when you test what you have learned in practice. You can now explain this, tell a concrete action from a vague one, and produce an action of your own. With structure, depth and action in place, your reflection can change what you do, not just what you think.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's response a concrete action rather than a vague intention?

items.text: It named exactly what to do and when: complete the treatment notes during the session, on a standard SOAP template.
It took the problem more seriously than Tom's response.
It showed more understanding of why marks were lost.
It was a stronger resolution to be careful.

feedback.correct: That's right. Naming exactly what to do, and when, is what makes it a concrete action.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the response that names exactly what to do and when.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's response was a concrete action because it named what to do and when. Taking the problem seriously, understanding it or resolving to be careful are not actions.
